column6: Moses carries tablets written on front and back; this adds a concrete two-faced writing surface to the commentary's material account of separately held sheets.
God says the sinner will be blotted from his book, joining Moses, a divine record, and the commentary's insistence that each person bears personal consequence.

column5: book placed as witness against turning away
column6: Moses' finished Torah book is placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel; it closely parallels former sheets invoked against a person who turns away from admonition.
The king must write a copy of Torah in a book, a distinct Mosaic instance of a later custodian making and retaining a textual witness.
The written copy remains with the king for continual reading so that he may learn fear of YHWH, joining page, recitation, and fear as S87's commentary does.

column5: life and good, death and evil
column6: Moses sets before Israel life with good and death with evil, a Mosaic moral choice that sharpens the commentary's two final outcomes.

column5: Abraham invokes God Most High and Creator
column6: Abraham himself names YHWH God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; it tightly joins the surah's Most High title with the commentary's Abrahamic Creator confession.
Abraham prays to God and healing follows, a narrative counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic sequence of invocation and the God who heals.

column5: Abraham rejects setting sun, moon, and stars
column6: This midrash makes Abraham consider celestial lights and reject them when they set, an exceptionally close Jewish interpretive parallel to the commentary's star-moon-sun scene.
Moses asks Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH; it directly frames Pharaoh's opposite response to the purifying, fear-producing call in the commentary.
The psalmist stores God's word in the heart, a concise Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's second custody of revelation in a memorizing heart.
Wisdom draws knowledge of the Maker from the greatness and beauty of creatures, supplying the Creator-side of the commentary's Abrahamic rejection of heavenly bodies.
Rain waters earth and makes it bud and sprout, a precise scriptural companion to the commentary's divine bringing forth of vegetation and pasture.
God's word goes out and accomplishes its purpose, giving the verbal counterpart to v10's rain and supporting the commentary's enduring effective speech on old pages.
The heavens are rolled up like a scroll at cosmic judgment, an exact Hebrew image for the commentary's contrast between unrolled sheets and a rolled sky.

column5: sky recedes like a rolling scroll
column6: Revelation reuses the sky-as-rolled-scroll image at the end, a Christian continuation of the commentary's eschatological page-and-cosmos imagery.

column5: scroll spread open, written front and back
column6: Ezekiel's spread scroll is inscribed on front and back with lamentation and woe, a vivid textual surface that carries warning rather than merely a book's title.

column5: words received in heart and ears
column6: After the scroll vision, Ezekiel is told to receive every spoken word in heart and hear it with ears; it supplies a distinct prophetic joining of internal memory and audible transmission.
Isaiah promises that the dead will live and sleepers in dust awaken, an explicit Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's other creation and final destination.

column5: King of the world raises to everlasting life
column6: A martyr suffering for ancestral law expects the King of the world to raise the faithful to everlasting life, a Jewish articulation of durable afterlife tied to inherited instruction.

column5: Mosaic divine name read as resurrection proof
column6: Jesus reads God's self-identification to Moses as proof that God is of the living, making a Mosaic text evidence for the resurrection taught in the former sheets.

column5: Scripture's message preached beforehand to Abraham
column6: Paul says Scripture proclaimed its good news beforehand to Abraham, a Christian way of locating later saving teaching already in an Abrahamic scriptural word.
Jesus declares that heaven and earth pass away but his words do not, a sharply stated Christian counterpart to the commentary's contrast between perishing creation and enduring speech.
The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, closely echoing the commentary's worldly preference versus what abides.
The final judgment separates people into eternal punishment and eternal life, a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's opposed enduring outcomes.

column5: scroll written inside and on back
column6: The heavenly scroll is written within and on its back before being opened, a Christian material image that complements the commentary's pages as visible, held, and unfolded writing.
